results.text:
[IMAGE_DIAGRAM: Table 15 | Page 35 | BBox (55, 55, 555, 700)]
- Visual Input Example (Table 15 — Ecole Polytechnique Physics Exam Question in French): Image of a French physics exam problem with a schematic diagram of a 1D conductive bar of length L along axis x, boundary temperatures T(0) = T0 at x=0 and T(L) = Tb at x=L.
- User prompt: 'Answer question I.1.a. Think step-by-step.'
- Solution derived from diagram & French text: Stationary 1D heat conduction equation d^2T/dx^2 = 0 -> T(x) = C1*x + C2. Applying boundary conditions T(0)=T0 and T(L)=Tb yields C2 = T0 and C1 = (Tb - T0)/L, so T(x) = (Tb - T0)*(x/L) + T0 (linear temperature profile with slope (Tb - T0)/L).

Table 15. Example prompt demonstrating GPT-4’s visual input capability. The prompt consists of a question which requires understanding a physics problem with a diagram written in French and solving it using chain-of-thought prompting.

GPT-4 visual input example, École Polytechnique Exam Question:
User Answer question I.1.a. Think step-by-step.
GPT-4 To answer question I.1.a, we need to express the temperature T(x) in every point of the conductive bar, which is characterized by the abscissa x. We are given that T(0) = T0 and T(L) = Tb.
For a stationary regime, the heat equation for the one-dimensional heat conduction in the bar is: d2T/dx2 = 0
Integrating once, we get: dT/dx = C1
Integrating a second time: T(x) = C1x + C2
To determine the constants C1 and C2, we use the boundary conditions: T(0) = T0, which gives C2 = T0 T(L) = Tb, which gives C1 = (Tb −T0)/L
Finally, the expression for T(x) is: T(x) = (Tb −T0) ∗(x/L) + T0 This represents a linear temperature profile along the conductive bar, with a slope of (Tb −T0)/L.

- Table 4 (TruthfulQA Examples): Left column shows GPT-4 answering correctly ('Can you teach an old dog new tricks?' -> 'Yes, you can teach an old dog new tricks'); Right column shows GPT-4 answering incorrectly to an adversarial trick question ('Son of an actor, this American guitarist and rock singer... His name is Elvis what?' -> GPT-4 picks 'Presley' instead of 'Perkins', i.e., Elvis Perkins, son of actor Anthony Perkins).
- Figure 7 Title: Accuracy on adversarial questions (TruthfulQA mc1). Y-axis: Accuracy (0% to 70%, higher is better).
- Models & conditions on X-axis: Anthropic-LM (0-shot ~30%, RLHF ~35%), gpt-3.5-base (0-shot ~28%, 5-shot ~29%), gpt-3.5-turbo (RLHF ~48%), gpt-4-base (0-shot ~30%, 5-shot ~41%), and gpt-4 after RLHF fine-tuning (~60%, highest bar).

[IMAGE_DIAGRAM: Table 17 | Page 37 | BBox (55, 55, 555, 720)]
- Visual Input Example (Table 17 — Pixel to Paper Summaries): Three page-screenshot images of the InstructGPT paper (including Figure 2 architecture diagram of the 3-step RLHF pipeline).
- User follow-up prompt on diagram: 'Could you explain the process described in Figure 2?'
- Three steps read from Figure 2 diagram in the screenshot:
  1. Supervised fine-tuning (SFT): Collect labeler demonstration data of prompts and desired output behavior to fine-tune GPT-3.
  2. Reward model (RM) training: Collect human labeler rankings of several model outputs from best to worst to train the reward model.
  3. Reinforcement learning using Proximal Policy Optimization (PPO): Optimize the SFT policy against the reward model using PPO.

[CHART: Figure 1 & Figure 2 | Page 3 | BBox (45, 55, 565, 680)]
- Figure 1 Title: OpenAI codebase next word prediction — Performance of GPT-4 and smaller models.
  Metric (y-axis): Final loss in Bits per word (range 1.0 to 6.0, lower is better) on an internal codebase dataset not in training set.
  X-axis: Training compute normalized so that GPT-4 = 1 (ticks: 100p, 10n, 1u, 100u, 0.01, 1). Series: Observed (dots) vs Prediction (dotted power-law fit to smaller models excluding GPT-4). GPT-4 final loss (~1.8 bits per word at compute=1) matches the power-law prediction.
- Figure 2 Title: Capability prediction on 23 coding problems — Performance of GPT-4 and smaller models on a subset of the HumanEval dataset (3rd easiest difficulty bucket).
  Metric (y-axis): -Mean Log Pass Rate (range 0 to 5). X-axis: Training compute normalized so that GPT-4 = 1 (ticks: 1u, 10u, 100u, 0.001, 0.01, 0.1, 1). Power-law fit to smaller models accurately predicts GPT-4 pass rate.

[CHART: Figure 4 | Page 6 | BBox (45, 55, 565, 430)]
- Figure 4 Title: Exam results (ordered by GPT-3.5 performance) — GPT performance on academic and professional exams.
- X-axis: Exams ordered from low to high based on GPT-3.5 performance (from AP Calculus BC, AMC 12, Codeforces Rating up to SAT EBRW, AP Environmental Science).
- Y-axis: Estimated percentile lower bound among test takers (0% to 100%). Legend: gpt-4 (dark green), gpt-4 no vision (light green), gpt3.5 (blue).
- Artifact explanation in caption: Reporting the conservative lower bound of percentile bins creates artifacts on AP exams with wide scoring bins — for example, although GPT-4 attains the highest possible score on AP Biology (5/5), it is shown in the plot as 85th percentile because 15% of test-takers achieve a 5.

Table 1. GPT performance on academic and professional exams. In each case, we simulate the conditions and scoring of the real exam. We report GPT-4’s final score graded according to exam- specific rubrics, as well as the percentile of test-takers achieving GPT-4’s score.
